findingTitles: tests/test_workflow_guard.py:15 Base-SHA checkout guard is evadable by formatting or extra keys

findingsDetail.title: Base-SHA checkout guard is evadable by formatting or extra keys
findingsDetail.body: The assertion checks for one exact YAML block, so a checkout that uses `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}` with reordered keys, different indentation, or an added `fetch-depth` (as this PR itself adds) will not match and the guard will pass while the vulnerability is present.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Parse the workflow YAML and assert that no checkout step sets `ref` to `${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}`, regardless of key order or extra options.

findingTitles: tests/test_workflow_guard.py:20 Guard test only verifies absence of exact literal, not behavioral protection

findingsDetail.title: Guard test only verifies absence of exact literal, not behavioral protection
findingsDetail.body: The test checks that a specific literal string is absent, but it will pass even if the workflow checks out the base SHA with different formatting (e.g., extra spaces, a template variable split across lines, or a different key order in the YAML), leaving the vulnerability unguarded. Since the test only asserts on the raw text, it would not fail when the supposed security property breaks through equivalent YAML syntax.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Parse the workflow YAML and assert that no step uses actions/checkout with a ref value referencing pull_request.base.sha, so the check holds regardless of formatting.

findingTitles: tests/test_workflow_guard.py:14 Guard test is evadable by YAML key ordering

findingsDetail.title: Guard test is evadable by YAML key ordering
findingsDetail.body: FORBIDDEN_CHECKOUT hard-codes an exact block without fetch-depth, so adding ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }} after the existing fetch-depth line will not match and the test still passes. The guard therefore does not fail when the forbidden checkout is introduced

findingTitles: tests/test_workflow_guard.py:29 Guard only inspects the `ref` input, not the checkout action's default

findingsDetail.title: Guard only inspects the `ref` input, not the checkout action's default
findingsDetail.body: The test asserts no base-ref token appears in the `ref` input, but a checkout step with no `ref` at all (or a `ref` that is empty) still checks out the base SHA by default, so the guard passes while the vulnerability remains.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Assert that every checkout step either omits `ref` entirely or sets it to a non-base value, and add a case where `ref` is absent to ensure the default is not silently accepted.

findingTitles: tests/test_workflow_guard.py:29 Guard passes vacuously when workflow has no checkout steps

findingsDetail.title: Guard passes vacuously when workflow has no checkout steps
findingsDetail.body: The new test asserts inspected > 0, but if the workflow file is malformed or the jobs key is missing, the loop yields nothing and the assertion fails — which is correct. However, the guard only inspects steps whose uses starts with 'actions/checkout'; if the workflow uses a different checkout action (e.g., a fork or a wrapper), the guard passes vacuously without inspecting any real checkout, silently allowing the vulnerability.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Fail the test if no checkout step is found, and consider asserting that at least one checkout step exists before the loop, or broaden the detection to any step that checks out code.

findingTitles: tests/test_workflow_guard.py:25 Guard does not cover input.sha/input.ref tokens

findingsDetail.title: Guard does not cover input.sha/input.ref tokens
findingsDetail.body: The real fix intends to break the base-SHA semantic token, yet BASE_REF_TOKENS omits the input.* form the change itself introduces, so the tests pass even if the code uses input.sha against base credentials.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Add the actual semantic token (e.g. inputs.sha / inputs.ref) to BASE_REF_TOKENS and assert it is rejected.

findingTitles: tests/test_workflow_guard.py:30 Guard passes vacuously when checkout step lacks a ref key

findingsDetail.title: Guard passes vacuously when checkout step lacks a ref key
findingsDetail.body: The test only inspects steps that have a `with.ref` value; a checkout step that omits `ref` entirely (defaulting to the head SHA) is never checked, so the guard would pass even if the workflow checks out a base ref via a different mechanism.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Assert that every checkout step has a `ref` key and that its value contains no base token, or fail if any checkout step is missing `ref`.

findingsDetail.title: Shared limiter state makes tests order-dependent
findingsDetail.body: The single `limiter` instance is shared across all three tests, so the suite only passes when run in declaration order; running the third test alone or in a different order fails, and the tests silently depend on execution order.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Instantiate a fresh `RateLimiter` inside each test (e.g., `const limiter = new RateLimiter({ max: 2 })` in each `it` block) so each test is independent.

findingsDetail.title: Test asserts on incidental event log rather than behavior
findingsDetail.body: The `expect(events).toEqual([...])` checks internal bookkeeping that is unrelated to rate limiting; it would fail on a harmless refactor and doesn't verify the limiter's behavior.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Remove the `events` array and the assertion on it; the `allow` return values already cover the behavior.

findingTitles: src/resolve_marker.js:15 Malformed marker is misreported as an empty body

findingsDetail.title: Malformed marker is misreported as an empty body
findingsDetail.body: When the body is non-empty but does not match MARKER_RE (for example, the retired `ct-review-bot:v1` marker the comment says should be rejected), the function throws 'marker unusable: the pull request body is empty'. This is misleading and the error message is factually wrong, which will make diagnosing the retired-marker case harder. The test suite only covers the empty-string path, so this branch is untested and the incorrect message would not be caught.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Distinguish the two failure cases: keep the empty-body check, then throw a distinct error for a non-matching marker, e.g. `throw new Error('marker unusable: unrecognized marker format')`. Add a test asserting that `resolveMarker('ct-review-bot:v1')` throws the new error.

findingTitles: src/resolve_marker.js:13 Malformed marker throws misleading 'empty body' error

findingsDetail.title: Malformed marker throws misleading 'empty body' error
findingsDetail.body: When the body is non-empty but does not match the marker regex (e.g. 'ct-review-bot:v1' or 'hello'), the code throws 'marker unusable: the pull request body is empty'. This is incorrect and misleading: the body is not empty, the marker is simply absent or retired. The error message will mislead debugging and the test suite does not cover this branch, so the misleading behavior can silently ship.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Distinguish the two failure cases: throw 'marker unusable: no supported marker found' (or similar) when the regex fails, and keep the empty-body message only for the falsy-body branch. Add a test for a non-empty body with an unsupported marker.

findingTitles: src/resolve_marker.js:12 No test covers the non-matching/retired-marker rejection branch

findingsDetail.title: No test covers the non-matching/retired-marker rejection branch
findingsDetail.body: resolveMarker now throws when body does not match MARKER_RE, but the only added test exercises the empty-body branch. The retired `ct-review-bot:v` marker named in the PR title and any other non-empty invalid body fall through to this untested branch; if it is removed or the regex is loosened, resolveMarker would return 0 for those payloads and the suite would still pass.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Add a test such as expect(() => resolveMarker('ct-review-bot:v1')).toThrow(/unusable/) and one for an arbitrary non-empty body, and consider distinguishing the error message for non-empty invalid bodies from the empty-body message.

findingTitles: src/resolve_marker.js:12 Untested invalid-marker rejection branch

findingsDetail.title: Untested invalid-marker rejection branch
findingsDetail.body: The new `if (!match)` branch is the entire rejection path for malformed or retired markers (e.g. `ct-review-bot:v1`). findingTitles: src/resolve_marker.js:15 Non-matching body throws a misleading error message

findingsDetail.title: Non-matching body throws a misleading error message
findingsDetail.body: When the body is non-empty but does not match MARKER_RE (e.g. the retired marker `ct-review-bot:v1`, or a body containing `review-yeti-bot:not-a-version`), the function throws `'marker unusable: the pull request body is empty'` even though the body is not empty. The error message is false in that condition-uniform branch. Just as importantly, the branch fails to reject the retired marker explicitly as the docstring claims; instead, any non-matching body collapses into the empty-body message, making the dual-cause failure misleading to callers who catch the error. The comment and the added test only cover the empty-string case, so the misleading diagnostic is the only behavior for the retired marker path and it asserts a false condition.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Split the two causes: `if (!body) { throw new Error('marker unusable: the pull request body is empty'); }` and then `if (!match) { throw new Error('marker unusable: the body has no usable marker'); }` (or explicitly `if (/^ct-review-bot:/u.test(body)) { throw new Error('marker unusable: retired marker'); }`). This makes the thrown message correspond to the actual cause and lets tests distinguish the retired-marker rejection from the empty-body rejection.

findingTitles: src/resolve_marker.js:12 Missing test for non-empty invalid marker branch

findingsDetail.title: Missing test for non-empty invalid marker branch

findingsDetail.suggestion: Add a test in `tests/resolveMarker.test.js` such as `expect(() => resolveMarker('ct-review-bot:v1')).toThrow('marker unusable')` (and/or `expect(() => resolveMarker('not a marker')).toThrow('marker unusable')`) to cover the non-empty invalid-marker path.

findingTitles: tests/unit/rateLimiter.test.ts:4 Shared limiter and events array make tests order-dependent

findingsDetail.title: Shared limiter and events array make tests order-dependent
findingsDetail.body: The RateLimiter instance and the events array are module-level shared state. The three tests rely on executing in declaration order: the first two calls must land before the third test asserts a block. If Vitest runs tests concurrently or in a different order, the third test fails (or the first two fail) even though the feature is correct. The events assertion also couples the third test to incidental side effects of the earlier tests rather than to the limiter's behaviour.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Create a fresh RateLimiter and a fresh events array inside each test (e.g. in beforeEach or at the top of each it), and drop the events assertion. For the burst-window behaviour, use a single test that performs the two allowed calls and then asserts the third is blocked, or use vi.useFakeTimers to control the window explicitly.

findingTitles: tests/unit/rateLimiter.test.ts:4 Shared mutable state and order-dependent tests

findingsDetail.title: Shared mutable state and order-dependent tests
findingsDetail.body: The `limiter` instance is created once at module scope and shared across all three tests, and the `events` array is also shared. The tests rely on execution order: the third test only passes if the first two tests ran first. If Vitest runs tests in isolation or in a different order, or if a test is skipped, the third test will fail. This makes the suite fragile and masks real behavior.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Create a fresh `RateLimiter` and `events` array inside each test (e.g., in a `beforeEach` or directly in each `it`), and avoid asserting on the shared `events` array. For example: `const limiter = new RateLimiter({ max: 2 });` inside each test.

findingTitles: tests/unit/rateLimiter.test.ts:15 Order-dependent test: module state and descriptive `it` names make Vitest run tests in a way that defeats the test's own assertion

findingsDetail.title: Order-dependent test: module state and descriptive `it` names make Vitest run tests in a way that defeats the test's own assertion
findingsDetail.body: The const `events = []`, `limiter = new RateLimiter({ max: 2 })`, and `events.push(...)` are all shared module-level state, and the mutations happen inside `it` callbacks. The third test uses `expect(events).toEqual(['first','second','third'])`, so if Vitest (or another runner) executes the `it` callbacks in a differing order — or if the file is ever split, filtered, or run with a stress/seed strategy — the `events` array will contain a different sequence of pushes than the three descriptive names implycpp. Crucially, none of the three `allow` calls is tied to this file or to `events`: all three refer to a singleton `RateLimiter` and the same `'key'`, so the module-level array plus order-descriptive `it` names makes the test assertion brittle and dependent on test-runner behavior.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Move the shared `RateLimiter` and event recording inside the `describe` so the state is per-describe and give each test a stable, order-independent assertion. For Vitest, use `describe.sequential` (or pass `--sequence.concurrent=false`/`--fileParallelism=false`) if the order genuinely must be `first, second, third`, and assert the result of `limiter.allow('key')` plus the returned status, not the `events` array order. Concretely: `const events: string[] = []; const limiter = new RateLimiter({ max: 2 }); describe('RateLimiter two-call burst', () => { it('first call passes and records order', () => { events.push('first'); expect(limiter.allow('key')).toBe(true); }); it('second call passes and records order', () => { events.push('second'); expect(limiter.allow('key')).toBe(true); }); it('third call blocks and records order', () => { events.push('third'); expect(limiter.allow('key')).toBe(false); expect(events).toEqual(['first','second','third']); }); }); and add `--sequence.sequential` to the Vitest run.

findingTitles: tests/unit/rateLimiter.test.ts:5 Shared mutable state and test order dependence

findingsDetail.title: Shared mutable state and test order dependence
findingsDetail.body: The tests share a single `limiter` instance and a shared `events` array across all three test cases. The assertions depend on the execution order: the first test consumes one allowance, the second consumes another, and the third expects the limiter to be exhausted. If tests are run in a different order or in isolation, the third test will fail. This violates the rule against shared mutable state between tests and creates order-dependent behavior.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Create a fresh `RateLimiter` instance and a fresh `events` array inside each test (e.g., using `beforeEach` or instantiating within each `it` block) to ensure test isolation and order independence.

If Vitest runs tests concurrently or in a different order, the third test fails (or the first two fail) even though the feature is correct. The events assertion also couples the third test to incidental side effects of the earlier tests rather than to the limiter's behaviour.
findingsDetail.suggestion: Create a fresh RateLimiter and a fresh events array inside each test (e.g. in beforeEach or at the top of each it), and drop the events assertion. For the burst-window behaviour, use a single test that performs the two allowed calls and then asserts the third is blocked, or use vi.useFakeTimers to control the window explicitly.
